```plato
    //==
    // # Distance constraints — projection and the Gauss-Seidel sweep
    //
    // The stretch constraint: keep two vertices `RestLength` apart. This is
    // the whole of a mass-spring cloth's structure, restated as a position
    // constraint instead of a force
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Position-based_dynamics).

    // The unweighted correction one distance constraint asks for: the
    // displacement that would remove the whole error if one end were free and
    // the other infinitely heavy. Each end then takes its own inverse-mass
    // share of it, with opposite signs.
    //
    // `Compliance` is an inverse stiffness in meters per newton and enters as
    // alpha = Compliance / dt^2, the XPBD softening term: zero is a rigid
    // constraint, larger values stretch. `stiffness` is the per-sweep
    // proportion of the error to remove — pass `IterationStiffness` so the
    // felt stiffness does not depend on the iteration count.
    //
    // Two fixed ends, or two coincident positions, ask for nothing.
    DistanceCorrection(vertices: Array<ClothVertex>, c: ClothDistanceConstraint, stiffness: Number, dt: Duration): Vector3D
    {
        var a = vertices[c.VertexA.Value];
        var b = vertices[c.VertexB.Value];
        var offset = a.Position - b.Position;
        var error = offset.Magnitude - c.RestLength.Meters;
        var alpha = SafeDivide(c.Compliance, dt.Seconds * dt.Seconds, 0.0);
        var share = a.SolverInverseMass + b.SolverInverseMass + alpha;
        return offset.NormalizeOr(Vector3D.Zero) * SafeDivide(error * stiffness, share, 0.0).Negative;
    }

    // One distance constraint projected: both ends displaced along the line
    // between them, each by its inverse-mass share of the correction, in a
    // single rebuild of the vertex array.
    ProjectDistance(vertices: Array<ClothVertex>, c: ClothDistanceConstraint, stiffness: Number, dt: Duration): Array<ClothVertex>
    {
        var a = vertices[c.VertexA.Value];
        var b = vertices[c.VertexB.Value];
        var correction = DistanceCorrection(vertices, c, stiffness, dt);
        return vertices.WithTwoVertices(c,
            a.Displaced(correction * a.SolverInverseMass),
            b.Displaced(correction * b.SolverInverseMass.Negative));
    }

    // One GAUSS-SEIDEL sweep over every distance constraint.
    //
    // This is the interesting line in the file. Gauss-Seidel projection is
    // defined by its sequencing: constraint k must see the corrections that
    // constraints 0 .. k-1 already made, which is why textbook implementations
    // write into one array in place. A LEFT FOLD has exactly that sequencing —
    // `Reduce` threads the whole vertex array through the constraint list, so
    // each projection reads the output of the previous one — and it is pure,
    // because each step returns a new array instead of writing a shared one.
    // The iteration order is the constraint array's own order, as it is in the
    // in-place version.
    //
    // Cost: one array rebuild per constraint (see the rewriting section above),
    // so O(vertices * constraints) per sweep against the in-place O(constraints).
    // The cheaper pure alternative is a JACOBI sweep — every constraint
    // evaluated against the same input and the per-vertex corrections averaged
    // — which needs only one rebuild for the whole sweep. It is not written
    // here because doing it in O(constraints) rather than
    // O(vertices * constraints) needs a per-vertex constraint adjacency table
    // this vocabulary does not build yet, and because Jacobi converges more
    // slowly per sweep and needs under-relaxation to stay stable, so it is a
    // different solver rather than a faster spelling of this one.
    SweepDistance(vertices: Array<ClothVertex>, constraints: Array<ClothDistanceConstraint>, stiffness: Number, dt: Duration)
        : Array<ClothVertex>
        => constraints.Reduce(vertices, (current, c) => ProjectDistance(current, c, stiffness, dt));

    // `iterations` Gauss-Seidel sweeps. Repetition is itself a fold: the range
    // supplies the count and the vertex array is threaded through it.
    SolveDistance(vertices: Array<ClothVertex>, constraints: Array<ClothDistanceConstraint>, iterations: Integer, stiffness: Number, dt: Duration)
        : Array<ClothVertex>
        => iterations.MapRange(i => i)
            .Reduce(vertices, (current, i) => SweepDistance(current, constraints, stiffness, dt));

    // The per-sweep stiffness that makes `iterations` sweeps feel like one
    // application of `stiffness`: k' = 1 - (1 - k)^(1/n), so the residual after
    // n sweeps is (1 - k') ^ n = 1 - k regardless of n. Without it, raising the
    // iteration count silently stiffens the cloth, and a demo that exposes an
    // iteration slider changes two things at once.
    // (Müller et al., Position Based Dynamics, 2007.)
    IterationStiffness(stiffness: Number, iterations: Integer): Number
        => iterations <= 0
            ? 0.0
            : 1.0 - (1.0 - stiffness.Saturate).Pow(SafeDivide(1.0, iterations.ToNumber, 1.0));

    //==
    // # Bend constraints — the dihedral projection
    //
    // A distance constraint two vertices apart resists folding only along one
    // axis and stiffens stretching as a side effect. The dihedral constraint
    // instead names the angle between the two triangles sharing an edge and
    // drives it toward `RestAngle`, which leaves stretching alone.
    //
    // Numbering follows `ClothBendConstraint`: VertexA and VertexB are the
    // shared edge, VertexC and VertexD the two wings. The normals are taken as
    // edge x wing from VertexA, so a FLAT pair — wings on opposite sides of the
    // edge — has the two normals opposed and a dihedral angle of pi. Rest
    // angles built from geometry (`ClothFromMesh`, below) carry that
    // automatically.
    // (Müller et al., Position Based Dynamics, 2007, §4.)

    // The unit normal of the triangle spanned by the shared edge and one wing,
    // both expressed as displacements from VertexA. Zero for a degenerate
    // triangle, which then contributes nothing.
    BendNormal(edge: Vector3D, wing: Vector3D): Vector3D
        => edge.Cross(wing).NormalizeOr(Vector3D.Zero);

    // The dihedral angle across the edge (p1, p2) between the triangles
    // (p1, p2, p3) and (p1, p2, p4), in [0, pi]. pi is flat.
    DihedralAngle(p1: Point3D, p2: Point3D, p3: Point3D, p4: Point3D): Angle
    {
        var edge = p2 - p1;
        var n1 = BendNormal(edge, p3 - p1);
        var n2 = BendNormal(edge, p4 - p1);
        return n1.Dot(n2).Clamp(-1.0, 1.0).Acos;
    }

    // The constraint gradient at one WING vertex: how the dihedral angle
    // changes as that wing moves. `ownNormal` is the normal of the triangle
    // this wing belongs to and `otherNormal` the other one.
    BendWingGradient(edge: Vector3D, wing: Vector3D, ownNormal: Vector3D, otherNormal: Vector3D, cosine: Number): Vector3D
        => (edge.Cross(otherNormal) + ownNormal.Cross(edge) * cosine)
            * SafeDivide(1.0, edge.Cross(wing).Magnitude, 0.0);

    // One triangle's contribution to the gradient at the SECOND shared-edge
    // vertex. The full gradient there is the negated sum of both triangles'
    // contributions; the first shared vertex's gradient is fixed by the
    // requirement that the four gradients sum to zero (a rigid translation
    // cannot change an angle).
    BendEdgeGradientTerm(edge: Vector3D, wing: Vector3D, ownNormal: Vector3D, otherNormal: Vector3D, cosine: Number): Vector3D
        => (wing.Cross(otherNormal) + ownNormal.Cross(wing) * cosine)
            * SafeDivide(1.0, edge.Cross(wing).Magnitude, 0.0);
```
